plain_english: Where is good? In your will. Where is evil? In your will. Where is neither good nor evil? In things that don't depend on your will. Okay, so does anyone think about these lessons outside of school? Does anyone practice giving answers to real situations the way we practice answering test questions? Like: Is it daytime? Yes. Is it nighttime? No. Is the number of stars even? I don't know. When someone offers you money, have you practiced giving the right answer — that money is not truly good? Have you trained yourself to respond correctly to real life, or just to clever arguments? So why are you surprised that you've improved in areas you've studied, but stayed the same in areas you haven't practiced?
original_excerpt: Where is the good? In the will. Where is the evil? In the will. Where is neither of them? In those things which are independent of the will. Well then? Does any one among us think of these lessons out of the schools? Does any one meditate (strive) by himself to give an answer to things as in the case of questions?—Is it day?—Yes.—Is it night?—No.—Well, is the number of stars even?—I cannot say.—When money is shown (offered) to you, have you studied to make the proper answer, that money is not a good thing? Have you practised yourself in these answers, or only against sophisms? Why do you wonder then if in the cases which you have studied, in those you have improved; but in those which you have not studied, in those you remain the same?
source_reference: Discourses, That We Do not Strive to Use Our Opinions About Good and Evil, Section 1

plain_english: A public speaker knows he wrote well. He memorized his speech and has a pleasant voice. So why is he still nervous? Because he's only studied one part of what he needs. What does he really want? To be praised by the crowd. He's trained himself to give speeches. But he's never trained himself to handle praise or criticism. When did anyone teach him what praise really is? What criticism is? What each one actually means? What kind of praise he should seek or what kind of blame he should avoid? When did he practice dealing with these things? So don't be surprised that he's great at what he's studied and ordinary at what he hasn't. It's like a musician who plays beautifully, sings well, and looks good. But he still shakes when he gets on stage. He knows his craft, but he doesn't understand crowds. He doesn't know what their cheers mean or what their mockery is. He doesn't even know what anxiety is — whether it's something he creates or something that just happens to him, whether he can stop it or not. That's why when people praise him, he leaves feeling puffed up. But when they mock him, he deflates like a punctured balloon.
original_excerpt: When the rhetorician knows that he has written well, that he has committed to memory what he has written, and brings an agreeable voice, why is he still anxious? Because he is not satisfied with having studied. What then does he want? To be praised by the audience? For the purpose then of being able to practise declamation he has been disciplined; but with respect to praise and blame he has not been disciplined. For when did he hear from any one what praise is, what blame is, what the nature of each is, what kind of praise should be sought, or what kind of blame should be shunned? And when did he practise this discipline which follows these words (things)? Why then do you still wonder, if in the matters which a man has learned, there he surpasses others, and in those in which he has not been disciplined, there he is the same with the many. So the lute player knows how to play, sings well, and has a fine dress, and yet he trembles when he enters on the stage; for these matters he understands, but he does not know what a crowd is, nor the shouts of a crowd, nor what ridicule is. Neither does he know what anxiety is, whether it is our work or the work of another, whether it is possible to stop it or not. For this reason if he has been praised, he leaves the theatre puffed up, but if he has been ridiculed, the swollen bladder has been punctured and subsides.
source_reference: Discourses, That We Do not Strive to Use Our Opinions About Good and Evil, Section 1

plain_english: This is how we are too. What do we admire? External things. What keeps us busy? External things. So why are we surprised that we're afraid and anxious? When we think the things coming our way are bad, what happens? We can't help being afraid. We can't help being anxious. Then we say, "God, how can I not be anxious?" You fool, don't you have hands? Didn't God give them to you? You don't sit down and pray for your nose to stop running. You wipe it yourself and don't blame God. So has God given you nothing for this situation? Hasn't he given you endurance? Hasn't he given you courage? Hasn't he given you strength? When you have such hands, do you still look for someone else to wipe your nose? But we don't study these gifts. We don't care about them.
original_excerpt: This is the case also with ourselves. What do we admire? Externals. About what things are we busy? Externals. And have we any doubt then why we fear or why we are anxious? What then happens when we think the things, which are coming on us, to be evils? It is not in our power not to be afraid, it is not in our power not to be anxious. Then we say, Lord God, how shall I not be anxious? Fool, have you not hands, did not God make them for you? Sit down now and pray that your nose may not run. Wipe yourself rather and do not blame him. Well then, has he given to you nothing in the present case? Has he not given to you endurance? Has he not given to you magnanimity? Has he not given to you manliness? When you have such hands do you still look for one who shall wipe your nose? But we neither study these things nor care for them.
source_reference: Discourses, That We Do not Strive to Use Our Opinions About Good and Evil, Section 1

plain_english: Show me someone who cares about how they do something, not just getting what they want. Show me someone who cares about their own effort. When you're walking around, do you care about your own energy? When you're making decisions, do you care about how you think through them? Or do you only care about getting what you're deciding about? If things work out, you get excited and say, "We thought this through so well! Didn't I tell you it had to turn out this way?" But if things go wrong, you're crushed. You don't even know what to say about what happened. Who among us has asked a prophet about this kind of thing? Who has lost sleep worrying about their own actions? Who? Give me a name. I want to see this person I've been searching for — someone who is truly noble and honest, whether young or old. Name them.
original_excerpt: Give me a man who cares how he shall do anything, not for the obtaining of a thing, but who cares about his own energy. What man, when he is walking about, cares for his own energy? Who, when he is deliberating, cares about his own deliberation, and not about obtaining that about which he deliberates? And if he succeeds, he is elated and says, How well we have deliberated; did I not tell you, brother, that it is impossible, when we have thought about anything, that it should not turn out thus? But if the thing should turn out otherwise, the wretched man is humbled; he knows not even what to say about what has taken place. Who among us for the sake of this matter has consulted a seer? Who among us as to his actions has not slept in indifference? Who? Give (name) to me one that I may see the man whom I have long been looking for, who is truly noble and ingenuous, whether young or old; name him.
source_reference: Discourses, That We Do not Strive to Use Our Opinions About Good and Evil, Section 1

plain_english: What weighs us down and disturbs us? What else but our opinions? What else weighs down someone who has to leave his friends, familiar places, and usual habits? Take little children — when their nurse leaves them for a bit, they cry. But give them a small cake and they forget all about it. Do you want us to compare you to little children? No way. I don't want you pacified by a small cake, but by right thinking. And what is right thinking? This: study all day long to not be affected by anything that isn't truly yours — not by friends, not by places, not by gyms, not even by your own body. Remember the law and keep it in front of your eyes. What is this divine law? Keep what is yours. Don't claim what belongs to others. Use what you're given. When it's not given, don't want it. When something is taken away, give it up quickly and willingly. Be grateful for the time you had it. Otherwise you'll cry for your nurse and mama.
original_excerpt: What then are the things which are heavy on us and disturb us? What else than opinions? What else than opinions lies heavy upon him who goes away and leaves his companions and friends and places and habits of life? Now little children, for instance, when they cry on the nurse leaving them for a short time, forget their sorrow if they receive a small cake. Do you choose then that we should compare you to little children? No, by Zeus, for I do not wish to be pacified by a small cake, but by right opinions. And what are these? Such as a man ought to study all day, and not to be affected by anything that is not his own, neither by companion nor place nor gymnasia, and not even by his own body, but to remember the law and to have it before his eyes. And what is the divine law? To keep a man's own, not to claim that which belongs to others, but to use what is given, and when it is not given, not to desire it; and when a thing is taken away, to give it up readily and immediately, and to be thankful for the time that a man has had the use of it, if you would not cry for your nurse and mamma.
source_reference: Discourses, That We Do not Strive to Use Our Opinions About Good and Evil, Section 1

plain_english: What difference does it make what controls you or what you depend on? How are you any better than someone who cries over losing a girl, if you're mourning the loss of your little gym, your little walkways, your young friends, and places like that where you have fun? Someone else comes along and complains that he can't drink from his favorite spring anymore. Is the new water source really worse than the old one? "But I was used to the old water." And you'll get used to the new water too. Then if you get attached to that one, you'll cry about losing it as well. You'll try to write dramatic poetry about it, like Euripides did: "The hot baths of Nero and the Marcian water." See how people turn ordinary events into tragedies when foolish people experience them?
original_excerpt: For what matter does it make by what thing a man is subdued, and on what he depends? In what respect are you better than he who cries for a girl, if you grieve for a little gymnasium, and little porticos, and young men, and such places of amusement? Another comes and laments that he shall no longer drink the water of Dirce. Is the Marcian water worse than that of Dirce? But I was used to the water of Dirce. And you in turn will be used to the other. Then if you become attached to this also, cry for this too, and try to make a verse like the verse of Euripides, The hot baths of Nero and the Marcian water. See how tragedy is made when common things happen to silly men.
source_reference: Discourses, That We Do not Strive to Use Our Opinions About Good and Evil, Section 1

plain_english: When will I see Athens again? When will I see the Acropolis? You fool — aren't you satisfied with what you see every day? Is there anything better or greater to see than the sun, the moon, the stars, the whole earth, the sea? If you truly understand the one who runs everything, and carry him within yourself, do you still crave little stones and a pretty rock?
original_excerpt: When then shall I see Athens again and the Acropolis? Wretch, are you not content with what you see daily? Have you anything better or greater to see than the sun, the moon, the stars, the whole earth, the sea? But if indeed you comprehend Him who administers the whole, and carry him about in yourself, do you still desire small stones and a beautiful rock?
source_reference: Discourses, That We Do not Strive to Use Our Opinions About Good and Evil, Section 1
